1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: Male patient, 63 years old, farmer, was admitted on Day 0 with the chief complaint of "recurrent fever with hematuria for 1 week." The patient developed fever 1 week before admission without an obvious precipitating cause, with a temperature of 37.7℃, accompanied by chills, rigors, and hematuria. The urine was tea-colored with foam, accompanied by low back pain, a sensation of lower abdominal distention/heaviness, generalized body aches, and mild cough without sputum. There was no urinary frequency, urgency, or dysuria, and no chest tightness, chest pain, or other discomfort. He visited a local clinic and was treated with oral antipyretic medication (specific drug unknown), but still had recurrent hematuria and fever, with the highest temperature reaching 39℃. Three days before admission, the patient presented to "a county hospital," where the following tests were performed: "CBC: WBC 10.20×10^9/L, N% 62.3%, MONO% 14.3%, L 2.35×10^9/L, MONO 1.46×10^9/L, HB 147g/L, PLT 139×10^9/L. CRP 55.60mg/L. PCT 1.54ng/ml. Urinalysis: red blood cell count 247.7/μl, white blood cell count 71.00/μl, bacterial count 422.6/μl. Chest + mid-abdomen + lower abdomen CT: 1. Suspicious ground-glass nodular lesion in the right middle lobe; 2. Mild emphysema of the right lung, bulla in the right upper lobe; 3. Multiple low-density lesions in both kidneys and the liver; 4. Accessory spleen? Status post splenectomy? 5. Multiple prostatic calculi or calcifications. Urinary tract color Doppler ultrasound: 1. Bilateral renal cysts with partial cyst wall calcification; 2. Benign prostatic hyperplasia with calculi; 3. No obvious postvoid residual urine in the bladder; 4. No obvious abnormality in the bilateral ureters or bladder." He was diagnosed with "urinary tract infection" and treated with cefoperazone/sulbactam for anti-infection and diclofenac sodium suppository for antipyresis, among other treatments. The urine color became clear, but he still had recurrent fever and generalized body aches. Since the onset of illness, his mental status has been fair, physical strength poor, appetite and food intake fair, sleep fair, no significant change in body weight, bowel movements normal, and urination as described above. Seventeen years ago, the patient underwent "splenectomy" at another hospital for traumatic splenic rupture caused by a motor vehicle accident. Occupation: farmer, with a history of living/traveling in mountainous and forest wilderness areas. Personal history and family history: unremarkable. Physical examination on admission: T: 39.0℃ P: 85 beats/min R: 20 breaths/min BP: 121/74mmHg. Alert and cooperative on examination. No jaundice or cyanosis of the skin or mucous membranes, no rash, no subcutaneous bleeding. No superficial lymphadenopathy palpable. Breath sounds clear in both lungs, with no dry or wet rales and no pleural friction rub. Regular heart rhythm, A2>P2, no murmur heard in any valve auscultation area, no pericardial friction rub. A left mid-abdominal oblique surgical scar approximately 15 cm in length was visible. Abdomen flat and soft, no tenderness or rebound tenderness throughout the abdomen, no palpable mass, liver and spleen not palpable below the costal margin, Murphy's sign negative. No percussion tenderness over the liver area, left renal percussion tenderness present, no right renal percussion tenderness. Bowel sounds 4 times/min, no succussion splash, no vascular bruit. No edema in either lower extremity. Pathologic reflexes were not elicited.

differential_diagnoses.name: Complicated urinary tract infection/acute pyelonephritis
supporting_evidence: Chief complaint: recurrent fever accompanied by hematuria for 1 week
Fever accompanied by chills and rigors, with a maximum temperature of 39°C
Accompanied by low back pain and a sensation of lower abdominal distension and bearing down
Left renal percussion tenderness
Urinalysis at the county hospital showed a red blood cell count of 247.7/μl, a white blood cell count of 71.00/μl, and a bacterial count of 422.6/μl
Inflammatory markers elevated: CRP 55.60mg/L, PCT 1.54ng/ml
Previously diagnosed with “urinary tract infection” at a county hospital
After cefoperazone-sulbactam use, "urine color became clear," suggesting that a urinary tract infection component may be present.
The presence of prostatic hyperplasia with calculi, multiple prostatic calculi, or calcifications is a predisposing factor for urinary tract infection.
opposing_evidence: No typical lower urinary tract irritative symptoms such as urinary frequency, urgency, and dysuria

Despite anti-infective treatment with cefoperazone-sulbactam, the patient continued to have recurrent fever and generalized body aches, suggesting that a simple common urinary tract infection cannot fully explain the condition.
Urinary system color Doppler ultrasound showed no obvious abnormalities in the bilateral ureters or bladder, and no obvious postvoid residual urine in the bladder

differential_diagnoses.name: Renal abscess/perirenal infectious focus
supporting_evidence: Persistent high fever, up to 39°C, accompanied by chills
Left costovertebral angle tenderness and low back pain suggest upper urinary tract or renal parenchymal involvement
Inflammatory markers were significantly elevated: CRP 55.60 mg/L, PCT 1.54 ng/ml
Recurrent fever persisted after initial anti-infective treatment, suggesting the possible presence of a focal infectious focus
CT showed multiple low-density lesions in both kidneys; although they were not characterized, the intrarenal low-density lesions need to be differentiated from infectious foci.
opposing_evidence: The information from the first stage did not provide direct evidence such as contrast-enhanced imaging demonstrating ring enhancement of the abscess, perirenal exudation, etc.
Peripheral blood WBC was only 10.20×10^9/L, without marked leukocytosis

differential_diagnoses.name: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (hantavirus infection)
supporting_evidence: Occupation: farmer; has a history of travel/living in mountainous and forested wilderness areas, with possible relevant epidemiologic exposure.
Initial symptoms were fever, chills, rigors, and generalized myalgia
Accompanied by hematuria; the urine was "meat-washing-water-like" foamy urine
with low back pain
Platelet count 139×10^9/L, although close to the lower limit of normal, shows a tendency toward mild reduction
opposing_evidence: Stage 1 information did not report hypotension, oliguria/anuria, significant renal dysfunction, or bleeding manifestations
Urinalysis showed elevated leukocyte and bacterial counts, further supporting a bacterial urinary tract infection.
Physical examination showed no rash or subcutaneous hemorrhage of the skin or mucous membranes.

differential_diagnoses.name: Leptospirosis or other zoonotic infections associated with outdoor exposure
supporting_evidence: Occupation: farmer, with a history of travel/living in mountainous and forested wilderness areas
Fever accompanied by chills and generalized body aches
with hematuria and low back pain
Inflammatory markers elevated: CRP 55.60mg/L, PCT 1.54ng/ml
Mild cough, may be seen in some systemic infections
opposing_evidence: In the first stage, the information provided did not include more typical clues such as a clear history of exposure to contaminated water, gastrocnemius tenderness, jaundice, or conjunctival congestion.
Urinalysis shows an elevated bacterial count, more consistent with a bacterial urinary tract infection
Physical examination showed no jaundice of the skin or mucous membranes.

differential_diagnoses.name: Urinary system tumor (kidney cancer/urothelial tumor of the renal pelvis or bladder) complicated by infection or bleeding
supporting_evidence: A 63-year-old man, in the higher-risk age group for urinary system tumors
Marked gross hematuria, described as "meat-washing-water-like foamy urine"
with low back pain
CT showed multiple low-density lesions in both kidneys, which need to be differentiated from renal space-occupying lesions.
Fever may be triggered by tumor necrosis, secondary infection, or hemorrhage.
opposing_evidence: This episode was characterized predominantly by fever, chills, elevated inflammatory markers, and increased urinary leukocytes/bacteria, which more strongly supports an infectious etiology.
Urinary system color Doppler ultrasound showed no obvious abnormalities in both ureters or the bladder, and no definite evidence of a mass was provided
After anti-infective treatment, the urine color cleared, which is not consistent with the typical presentation of persistent neoplastic hematuria.

recommended_exams.exam: routine tests of blood, urine, and stool
CT urography of the bilateral kidneys, ureters, and bladder

differential_diagnoses.name: Urinary tract infection and drug-induced kidney injury
evidence: Recurrent fever, accompanied by hematuria and low back pain; based on the blood counts, inflammatory markers, urinalysis, etc., "urinary tract infection" is highly likely.

Before and after admission, diclofenac sodium suppositories and loxoprofen were administered sequentially for antipyretic and anti-inflammatory treatment; the possibility of drug-induced kidney injury should be considered with caution.
exclusion_reasons: Cannot explain the full clinical picture; despite sequential changes in antibiotics for anti-infective treatment, the fever peak did not decrease. There has been no recurrent fever in recent days; it is considered that the disease causing the fever may be self-limited.

differential_diagnoses.name: Hemolytic anemia
evidence: Hemoglobin decreased significantly over a short period of time, accompanied by renal injury; the possibility of hemolysis should be considered.
exclusion_reasons: The patient has no obvious jaundice, no significant abnormality in bilirubin, and insufficient evidence of hemolytic anemia.

differential_diagnoses.name: Multiple myeloma
evidence: Possible cause of fever, anemia, and renal impairment
exclusion_reasons: Based on the patient's bone marrow aspiration report and PET-CT results, a plasma cell disorder is not supported.

differential_diagnoses.name: epidemic hemorrhagic fever
evidence: May cause fever and kidney injury
exclusion_reasons: Fever is often proportional to the progression of renal failure, and thrombocytopenia and a bleeding tendency are common; this is inconsistent with that.

exclusion_reasons: There is no evidence of involvement of the lungs or other sites, and ANCA is negative, which is not consistent with ANCA-associated vasculitis.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Peripheral blood smear: schistocytes 0.2%; suspected Plasmodium/Babesia detected.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient presented with recurrent high fever, chills, diffuse body aches, and hematuria, followed by progression to a marked decline in hemoglobin over a short period (from 147 g/L to 109 g/L and then to 62 g/L), significantly elevated LDH, oliguria, and acute kidney injury with creatinine 716 umol/L, suggesting acute hemolysis with renal involvement. The patient was post-splenectomy and had a history of mountain/forest outdoor exposure, making him a high-risk host for tick-borne blood parasitic infections such as babesiosis. Early empiric antibacterial treatment for urinary tract infection could transiently clear the urine color, but recurrent fever, negative cultures, and the inability of routine infection to explain the progressive anemia and renal failure indicated the need to investigate atypical pathogens. A peripheral blood smear can directly detect intraerythrocytic parasites and red blood cell destruction, while also identifying schistocytes, helping explain manifestations of hemolytic uremic syndrome and differentiate from simple urinary tract infection, drug-induced kidney injury, immune-mediated hemolysis, hematologic disease, and malaria. This test is rapid and direct, and is an important basis for identifying key clues to babesiosis, promoting subsequent etiologic confirmation, and initiating targeted antiparasitic treatment as early as possible.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Babesia microti (BM) nucleic acid test was sent: positive.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: After suspected Plasmodium/Babesia organisms have been identified on peripheral blood smear, further molecular testing is needed for etiologic confirmation. This patient has no history of overseas residence or travel but does have mountain/forest outdoor exposure history and is a post-splenectomy host, presenting with persistent high fever, chills, hematuria, progressive severe anemia, elevated LDH, and acute renal failure; clinically, these findings are highly consistent with severe babesiosis and hemolysis-related organ injury. Because blood smear morphology can be confused with Plasmodium and other intraerythrocytic parasites, and the level of parasitemia may fluctuate, nucleic acid testing can improve specificity and sensitivity and address the key clinical question of whether this is Babesia infection and provide specific pathogen confirmation. Once BM positivity is confirmed, the etiology can be further narrowed from differentials such as common bacterial infection, drug-induced kidney injury, immune-mediated or microangiopathic hemolysis to Babesia infection, which helps establish the final diagnosis, determine that this is a severe case, promptly select targeted treatment such as atovaquone plus azithromycin, and provide a clear etiologic basis for supportive treatment such as continued dialysis.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: Peripheral blood smear: schistocytes 0.2%; suspected Plasmodium/Babesia detected. In conjunction with the patient being a farmer, having a history of living in mountainous/forest wilderness areas, and no history of travel abroad, Babesia microti (BM) nucleic acid testing was sent: positive.
